justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a broadly stable near-term outlook with a slight upward drift over longer horizons. For the one-day estimate, I anchored closely to the prevailing market price, assuming mean-reversion dynamics and no imminent catalysts that would dramatically reprice the asset overnight. The modest upward bias in the one-week and one-month estimates reflects a general assumption of a mild positive drift, consistent with the long-run tendency of risk assets to grind higher in the absence of acute shocks. The incremental increases across horizons are intentionally small because I see no compelling directional signal strong enough to justify a more aggressive trend forecast.

Confidence interval widths expand naturally with the forecast horizon, reflecting the compounding of uncertainty over time. At the one-day level, intraday liquidity and market-making tend to contain price swings, so my 90% interval is relatively tight. By the one-week horizon, weekend gaps, macro data releases, and sentiment shifts meaningfully widen the range of plausible outcomes. At one month, I incorporated the possibility of earnings announcements, central bank decisions, geopolitical developments, and broader market regime changes, all of which can interact in non-linear ways and push volatility well above its recent baseline.

Several tail risks could easily push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macro conditions — an unexpected inflation print, a credit event, or an escalation in geopolitical tensions — could drive prices well below my lower bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon. On the upside, a positive surprise such as a stronger-than-expected economic release, dovish policy pivot, or short-squeeze dynamic could carry prices above my upper bounds. Liquidity conditions also matter; a thin market can amplify moves that would otherwise be absorbed.

It is worth noting that my intervals, while wide by typical standards, are still parametric assumptions rather than guarantees. Fat-tailed distributions in financial markets mean that events outside a 90% confidence interval occur more frequently than classical statistics would suggest. Structural breaks — a change in market microstructure, a flash crash, or an unexpected regulatory announcement — represent the category of risk most likely to invalidate my forecasts entirely, as these are the scenarios that no backward-looking volatility estimate adequately captures.
